source.title: Stable and Steerable Sparse Autoencoders with Weight Regularization

record.file_problem: The text is a full paper, including appendices; no apparent garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures learned-feature consistency and decoder geometry in overcomplete sparse autoencoders, using methods different from the original toy-model superposition experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on SAE feature consistency, decoder geometry, and steering. Steering results are recorded under fits_no_version because steering success and its correlation with auto-interpretability do not directly measure any listed claim version. SAEBench metrics are mentioned, but the text does not provide their specific results in a form bearing on these versions. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures cross-seed reproducibility of SAE features on Pythia-70M residual-stream activations, standard and L2-regularized. This bears directly on V5's claim that dictionary features are stable units. The method differs from the original: SAE seed matching rather than toy-model training. The paper's main aim is a method improvement, but it reports the unregularized SAE baseline alongside its own method.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that L2 weight regularization increases cross-seed SAE feature sharedness and steering success (among explained features) while collapsing many latents. They interpret it as complexity control or implicit effective-dictionary-size selection, with effects that depend on the training recipe and architecture.
record.recipe_differences: This study trains and evaluates sparse autoencoders with weight regularization, cross-seed feature matching, and steering; it does not reproduce the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effects vary with regularization, sparsity k, SAE architecture, tied versus untied initialization, decoder unit-norm constraints, and whether only alive features are considered. Steering was evaluated at k=40; the steering result is conditional on valid auto-interpretability explanations.

fits_no_version.finding: MNIST pixel SAEs: cross-seed strict sharedness is ≈0% without constraints. It reaches 22.5% of alive features with tied initialization, unit-norm decoder and L2 (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-seed stability of dictionary learning depends strongly on initialization, decoder constraints and weight regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: L2 lowers mean absolute pairwise cosine of SAE decoder columns; surviving features drop below the random reference (~0.035) at k≥80.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight regularization makes SAE dictionaries more orthogonal than random at moderate-to-high k.

fits_no_version.finding: At k=40, L2 roughly doubles steering success (6.3%→13.0%) among features with valid explanations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: L2 regularization can increase steering success among explained SAE features.

fits_no_version.finding: The Spearman correlation between auto-interp score and steering success rises from 0.060 to 0.144 with L2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularization strengthens the link between explanation quality and controllability.

record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, 2026; arXiv.org
record.problems: Language-model experiments use only Pythia-70M-deduped. Cross-seed and steering analyses focus on TopK; steering is evaluated only at k=40 and uses a single LLM judge. The L2 TopK models have a high dead-feature rate, and the authors state that they did not directly compare regularized SAEs with smaller unregularized dictionaries. The evidence does not establish that SAE features are complete or canonical representations.
record.rows_left_out: The table's remaining MNIST consistency measures (mean max cosine, fraction paired, and fraction shared among all features) are not separately included; the rows retain the strict shared-feature measures most directly relevant to cross-seed stability. No other numerical results bearing on the listed versions were identified.

untested.parts: Completeness of SAE features; whether they are canonical across dictionary sizes or architectures (cross-seed tests ran on TopK only, Pythia-70M only).
Not tested: no toy superposition network, sparsity transition or feature geometry.
Not tested: SAEs are trained, but whether they recover the model's true features is not assessed.

missing.what: Separate rows for unregularized Pythia TopK cross-seed metrics (shared <2%, mean max cos ≤0.32, paired <10%), per k if readable from the figure.
Alive-feature counts showing the stability gain comes with dictionary collapse (16,384 alive unregularized vs 1,699 with L2; ~14,822 dead).

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked SAE decoder geometry to V1 and MNIST pixel SAEs to V5. Neither concerns a model's internal features, so both were relinked to none. Only the Pythia cross-seed results bear on V5, and their unregularized baseline is the stronger evidence against stability. Regularized gains are the study's own method and stay partial. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures SAE decoder geometry, not whether a network's underlying sparse features are stored as superposed directions. It does not test a sparsity-dependent transition in toy networks, feature co-activation, or importance-dependent allocation.
Neuron polysemanticity and competition for dedicated versus shared capacity are not measured.
The study does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
It does not measure whether model features are distributed across neurons or establish that SAEs recover the model's underlying sparse features.
The study measures cross-seed feature consistency, but does not establish that SAE features are complete representations or canonical units.
The study does not test whether underlying model features are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

relation.reason: The study measures reproducibility of learned dictionary features across independently trained SAEs, directly bearing on V5.

tranche.reason: Cross-seed SAE feature matching directly tests V5 stability using a different method from the original toy-model superposition experiments.

source_check.notes: Alive means encoder–decoder cosine >0.1; strict sharing requires agreeing encoder/decoder Hungarian matches with both similarities >0.7. The exact alive pools of 1,699 versus 16,384 and approximately 90% latent collapse concern k=40; completeness and canonicality are not directly tested.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Pythia-70M-deduped TopK SAE decoder geometry at k=40 and k=320, with and without L2 regularization
reader_labels.reason: The measured decoder geometry is conditional on sparsity and regularization: at k=40 alive-feature cosine values are nearly identical, while at k=320 L2 survivors are more orthogonal (r28–r30). The paper does not test the full toy-model storage claim.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: L2-regularized MNIST and Pythia-70M-deduped TopK SAEs
reader_labels.reason: Regularization increases cross-seed sharedness, including 22.50% of alive MNIST features under tied initialization and unit-norm decoders and an aggregate increase from < 2% to ∼35% for Pythia (r24–r25).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: All reported MNIST configurations and Pythia TopK settings
reader_labels.reason: Sharedness is low or modest in several conditions, and even the best MNIST alive-feature shared fraction is 22.50%; this supports improved reproducibility, not complete or canonical feature units (r13–r24).
